description: Design a data structure that follows the constraints of a Least Recently Used (LRU) cache. Implement get(key) and put(key, value) each in O(1) time.
intuition: No single data structure gives you both O(1) lookup and O(1) eviction of the least-recently-used item. The trick is combining two: a hash map for instant key lookup and a doubly linked list to maintain usage order. Every access moves a node to the front, so the back is always the least-recently-used item ready to evict.
approach: Combine a hash map (for O(1) lookup) with a doubly linked list (for O(1) insertion/removal). The list maintains usage order: most recently used at front, least recently used at back.
code:
class Node:
    def __init__(self, key: int = 0, val: int = 0):
        self.key = key
        self.val = val
        self.prev = None
        self.next = None

class LRUCache:
    def __init__(self, capacity: int):
        self.cap = capacity
        self.cache = {}  # key -> Node
        self.head = Node()  # dummy head
        self.tail = Node()  # dummy tail
        self.head.next = self.tail
        self.tail.prev = self.head

    def _remove(self, node: Node):
        node.prev.next = node.next
        node.next.prev = node.prev

    def _add_to_front(self, node: Node):
        node.next = self.head.next
        node.prev = self.head
        self.head.next.prev = node
        self.head.next = node

    def get(self, key: int) -> int:
        if key not in self.cache:
            return -1
        node = self.cache[key]
        self._remove(node)
        self._add_to_front(node)
        return node.val

    def put(self, key: int, value: int) -> None:
        if key in self.cache:
            self._remove(self.cache[key])
        node = Node(key, value)
        self.cache[key] = node
        self._add_to_front(node)
        if len(self.cache) > self.cap:
            lru = self.tail.prev
            self._remove(lru)
            del self.cache[lru.key]

LRUCache(capacity=2)
List state: HEAD <-> TAIL

put(1, 1):
  Insert node(1,1) at front
  List: HEAD <-> [1,1] <-> TAIL,  cache: {1->node}

put(2, 2):
  Insert node(2,2) at front
  List: HEAD <-> [2,2] <-> [1,1] <-> TAIL,  cache: {1,2}

get(1):
  Found key=1, move its node to front
  List: HEAD <-> [1,1] <-> [2,2] <-> TAIL
  Return 1

put(3, 3):  (capacity exceeded)
  Insert node(3,3) at front
  List: HEAD <-> [3,3] <-> [1,1] <-> [2,2] <-> TAIL
  Evict LRU (tail.prev = node(2,2))
  List: HEAD <-> [3,3] <-> [1,1] <-> TAIL,  cache: {1,3}

get(2): key not in cache -> return -1
explanation:
- The hash map gives O(1) access to any node by key.
- The doubly linked list maintains recency order (most recent at head, least recent at tail).
- On get: move the accessed node to the front (mark it as most recently used).
- On put: insert/update the node at front. If over capacity, evict the node at tail (LRU).
- Dummy head/tail sentinels eliminate null-check edge cases in remove/add operations.
timeComplexity: Constructor: O(1); get: O(1); put: O(1)
hints: You need O(1) lookup AND O(1) eviction. One data structure alone can't do both.
A hash map gives O(1) lookup; a doubly linked list gives O(1) insertion and removal.
Combine them: the map stores key -> node, the list maintains usage order.
